title: The Nihangs
hook: blue-robed Sikh orders who keep the old martial traditions alive

segments.voice: Yesterday, gatka, the moving prayer. Your line was move with prayer. Did one walk or chore get a word in the breath? Today, the people who never stopped living the old martial ways. Day two hundred eighty.

Anandpur, in spring, at Hola Mohalla. Out of the dust come riders on horseback, standing in the stirrups at a gallop, spears raised. They wear deep blue robes. Their turbans are enormous, stacked high, and ringed with small steel circles and emblems that flash in the sun. It looks like a scene from three hundred years ago, and in a way it is. These are the Nihangs. Today we meet them, and then look back on a week of sword and saint.
screen: `ANANDPUR, IN SPRING.` → `RIDERS IN DEEP BLUE.` → `TURBANS RINGED WITH STEEL.`

segments.voice: The Nihangs are orders of Sikh warriors who keep the Khalsa's old martial life going. They're sometimes called Akali Nihangs, from Akal, the Timeless: the ones who belong to the Timeless. They wear blue, a color tradition links to Guru Gobind Singh. They tie the tall turban called a dumalla, often carrying small steel weapons and quoits, the chakkar, in its folds. They keep horses, train with traditional weapons, and many live a traveling, communal life in their camps, called chhaunis. In the eighteenth century, when the Khalsa was fighting to survive, Nihang bands were among its fiercest defenders. Where the name comes from, sources give different answers. Some explain it from a Persian word for a crocodile, a creature fearless in the water. Others from roots meaning without fear, or without attachment. Nobody can settle it, and each explanation says something Nihangs value. Not every Sikh lives like a Nihang, and the Nihangs are a small part of the panth. But at Hola Mohalla, the spring gathering tradition traces to Guru Gobind Singh at Anandpur, it's the Nihangs' riding and mock battles that much of the crowd comes to see. Now look back at this week. The saint-soldier, prayer and courage in one person. Piri, the spirit a little higher. The kirpan, mercy first. Zafarnama: every other means first. Dharam yudh: fair, even in conflict. Gatka: move with prayer. And the Nihangs: the old ways kept. Tomorrow, the last day of this stretch, and the fight the Gurus cared about most.
screen: `AKALI NIHANGS — THOSE OF THE TIMELESS.` · `BLUE ROBES, TALL DUMALLA, HORSES.` · `A NAME WITH MANY EXPLANATIONS.` · `A WEEK OF SWORD AND SAINT.` · then, large: `THE OLD WAYS KEPT.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who keeps an old way alive. A grandparent who still cooks the family dish from memory. A neighbor who mends instead of throwing away. A friend who still writes letters by hand. Picture them doing it. Notice the patience in it, and what would be lost if nobody did. If you like, choose one old way of your own you'd like to keep going. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Nihang. The blue-robed Sikh warrior orders who keep the Khalsa's old martial traditions alive, on horseback, in camps, and at Hola Mohalla.
Your line: the old ways kept. Today, thank someone who keeps an old tradition alive, or keep one yourself for an hour. Day two hundred eighty.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Nihang; explained variously as crocodile (Persian), fearless, or unattached.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Sikh costume for festivals.
what it means: living orders of Sikh warriors who keep the Khalsa's old martial life all year round.

what a scholar hears: also called Akalis, 'those of the Timeless'; organized historically into dals such as the Budha Dal; the name's etymology is disputed between Persian nihang (crocodile) and Indic roots for fearless or unattached.
